Closed-Loop Sloshing Control
LiquidSloshingRL · Capstone Progress

Teaching a Tank to Damp Its Own Sloshing—Then Proving It Against Real Fluid

An RL policy learns to suppress liquid sloshing using a fast analytical fluid model, then gets validated against a real particle-based CFD simulation (Chrono::FSI/SPH) built from source on this machine. This page tracks what's actually been confirmed, end to end.

Sloshing suppression: solved (Phase 9–11) Real SPH fluid physics: running locally (Phase 13–14) Best closed-loop policy found & benchmarked vs. PID/LQR (Phase 15; stable ~5 s, a stated bound) Hardware-deployable (pressure-only) control: evaluated, negative — on hold (out of current scope)
◆

At a glance: the results in plain words

A water tank sits on a single pivot and a motor tilts it. A learned controller (reinforcement learning) decides, 50 times a second, how hard to twist the tank so the water stops sloshing. It was trained on a fast simplified water model, then tested on realistic particle-simulated water. This is a summary only: every detailed figure and number below is unchanged.

1.2 s
Time for the learned controller to calm the sloshing on the simplified model. The formula-based LQR controller takes 3.4–3.7 s; a standard PID controller does not react at all, because it cannot see the water.
15× less
Sloshing energy left by the learned controller on realistic water, compared with PID (0.0010 J vs 0.0157 J).
0.7 s
How long LQR lasted on realistic water before losing control. A controller built on a simplified model can fail on the real physics.
~5 s
How long the learned controller stays in control on realistic water. After that it loses control too; this is reported as a known limit, not hidden.
3.8×
Improvement from a short fine-tune on realistic tank physics. Training longer made it worse, so stopping early matters.
within 6%
How closely the simple pendulum model predicts the realistic water’s sloshing frequency (1.34 vs 1.42 Hz). The realistic simulation itself converges: the error halves with each finer grid.
00

How the whole system fits together

One pluggable interface (FluidBackend) lets the same RL environment run against three fluid models of increasing physical fidelity—without changing the environment code between them.

Why control is needed
The tank's centre of mass sits 119 mm above the pivot, so gravity tips it further over rather than pulling it back: the term (mtht + mihi)·g·θ is destabilising, like an inverted pendulum. That is why the tank needs active control at all. The fast training surrogate leaves this gravity term out (and forces its pendulum through dθ/dt only); the real-physics Chrono tank and the real-fluid SPH simulations include it.

02

Validating the fluid model against real SPH

The pendulum model that made training fast is only an approximation of real fluid behavior. A from-source Chrono::FSI build (real smoothed-particle-hydrodynamics fluid) now runs locally on this machine—the first time in this project's history outside a borrowed Colab GPU— and lets the approximation be checked against ground truth directly.

Real finding
The Housner approximation genuinely diverges from real fluid, for two distinct and now-understood reasons—not a bug either time. This is exactly the kind of result a validation study should produce.

A separate question from "does SPH agree with the pendulum model" is "does SPH agree with itself as particle resolution changes"—the standard numerical-convergence check any mesh/particle-based solver needs. Run locally on the RTX 3090 machine (a full from-source Chrono::FSI build completed and parity-checked against the second machine's own build first), the same tank motion was replayed through SPH at FOUR particle spacings: 0.010 m (~1,846 particles, this project's long-standing default), 0.005 m (~14,800 particles), 0.003 m (~68,000 particles), and 0.002 m (~2,258,100 particles, ~9.1 hours of real GPU time).

Real finding — genuine numerical convergence, not just resolution-sensitivity
The gap between consecutive refinements roughly halves each time as resolution increases—dx=0.010 vs 0.005: 1.40 mm mean, dx=0.005 vs 0.003: 0.70 mm, dx=0.003 vs 0.002: 0.35 mm. That near-perfectly geometric shrinking gap is the real signature of a converging numerical solution, not merely "results change with resolution." Independently: dx=0.005 (−10.0 mm), dx=0.003 (−10.6 mm), and dx=0.002 (−10.9 mm) final settled positions cluster together and are still visibly converging toward roughly −11 mm, while dx=0.010's final position (−39.2 mm) is a clear outlier that hadn't even reached that value by the point the finer runs had already settled. This project's long-standing default resolution (dx=0.010, used for every training run and prior SPH comparison) is confirmed genuinely under-resolved for high-fidelity fluid-position accuracy, though it remains adequate for the qualitative validation work earlier in this section.
03

Closing the loop against real fluid

The same already-trained policy, making live torque decisions against genuine two-way-coupled SPH fluid—the fluid's real force affects the tank, which the policy then reacts to. No retraining from scratch: SPH is too slow for that. This is a deployment/fine-tuning test of an existing solution against harder physics, not a new model.

Real recorded data, not a live simulation: tank rotation from the measured tank_angle, the amber dot from the measured fluid center-of-mass offset (fluid_com_x/y, tank-local frame)—a single-point summary of the fluid, useful for exact scrubbing through values. The shaded body is the fluid drawn from that same real tank_angle: its free surface is held LEVEL in world space and volume-conserving as the tank rotates, because real liquid under gravity pools into the low corner rather than tilting with its container. That the real data agrees with this is checkable here: a level surface in a tank tilted by a forces the tank-local fluid COM to tan(a)·A²/(3h), and early in this run the measured fluid_com_x matches that to 0.1 mm (−0.0127 vs −0.0126 m). By the end it reaches 10× it — 66% of the tank's half-length while the tank angle barely moves, which no level surface can do. That divergence is the wall-penetration degradation discussed just below, which is why the drawn surface follows the measured angle rather than the measured COM. Fig. 5 above shows what the real particle field actually looked like for this kind of run.

Corrected
The "~34% of particles freeze" finding above (originally logged as an open, unconfirmed mystery) turned out to be a measurement artifact, not a real solver behavior — caught while fixing the mess a follow-up 3D visualization made obvious. Root cause: a real bug in the capture script let it keep simulating and recording particle snapshots for dozens of steps after a safety trip should have stopped it, so 48 of the animation's 80 captured frames reflected an already-destabilized run, not real physics. The "freeze" check measured movement across the run's second half — which, unfixed, was entirely inside that invalid tail. Re-measured on just the real, valid portion (the first 32 frames, steps 0–159): only 1.2% of markers (23 of 1,846) freeze — back in the same rare-artifact range already seen and understood in earlier runs (Entries 45–46), not a new phenomenon needing an artificial_viscosity explanation. No further investigation needed here; the capture script is fixed so this can't recur silently.
Confirmed
A second, separate issue in Fig. 5: at a few points in the run, real fluid markers sit measurably outside the tank's actual walls—not a plotting artifact. Checked directly against the raw captured positions (offline, no GPU needed): inverse-rotating every particle into the tank's own frame at each frame's real tank_angle and comparing against the tank's real interior bounds shows 15 of 32 valid frames with particles outside, concentrated at t=1.00–1.16s (up to 476 of 1,846 markers, by as much as 2.5 cm—over two particle-spacings) during a stretch where the tank angle reverses direction rapidly. Tracking individual escaped particles frame-by-frame shows they re-enter the tank within 2–3 control steps rather than staying outside permanently—a transient boundary penetration, not a hole in the container or a leak that grows. These are genuine fluid-classified markers (the same GetNumFluidMarkers()-sliced convention already confirmed correct elsewhere in this project), not misclassified boundary/BCE points. Best-supported explanation: the ADAMI boundary method allowing brief penetration when the wall itself is accelerating hard enough to locally violate the boundary's own stability margin—consistent with, but distinct from, the already-documented CFL fix (Entry 55) and the stuck-particle question above. Not yet fixed; logged as a real, open solver-fidelity issue (the development log Entry 61).
Tested a fix
Four real candidate fixes have now been tried for the wall-penetration issue above—three parameter tweaks around the existing ADAMI boundary method (lower artificial viscosity, finer step size, more boundary-marker layers), all closed negative, and one genuinely different boundary method entirely: Chrono::FSI's HOLMES boundary treatment. Tested head-to-head against ADAMI on the exact checkpoint/settings that produced the original finding: HOLMES cuts wall penetration by roughly 8.5× (deepest penetration 2.54 cm → 0.30 cm, worst-frame violation 63.9% → 16.8%) — a real fix for containment specifically — but the policy also survives meaningfully less long under it (160 → 116 steps on this checkpoint; confirmed in the same direction on a second checkpoint too). Since that policy was trained entirely under ADAMI dynamics, the open question at this point was whether that was a fair test—would a policy trained under HOLMES from the start do better? Answered below.
Answered — HOLMES closed, negative
A full training campaign (16,384 timesteps, warm-started from the same base policy the original ADAMI campaign used, for a fair comparison) hit a real, reproducible problem twice, at two independent checkpoints: the policy converged onto an action sequence that deterministically crashed the SPH solver—confirmed by near-identical state trajectories across three different random seeds each time, all failing at almost the same step. A bounded test at a lower torque limit (5.0 vs. the established 7.0 N·m) made this worse, not better—crashing before even the first checkpoint —ruling out torque tuning as the fix. Training was closed at 4,096/16,384 steps (25%) as the honest result. A full sweep of every checkpoint produced, plus (for reference) the best-known ADAMI checkpoint (514560) evaluated under HOLMES, settled the question completely: not one clean evaluation—from any checkpoint, under either training regime— controlled the tank well under HOLMES. Even 514560 showed wildly inconsistent behavior run-to-run under HOLMES with identical settings (final tilt 23°, 28°, and 202° across three attempts)—real chaotic sensitivity to GPU floating-point noise that ADAMI never showed. Conclusion: HOLMES is not a usable improvement over ADAMI for this project's control task, in either direction. ADAMI remains the default, and 514560 remains this project's only validated closed-loop checkpoint.

tank angle torque slosh kinetic energy safety stop
Honest read
Control is genuinely good through ~step 150 (angle held near −0.18 to −0.20 rad, torque working hard against real fluid forces)—then angular velocity crosses the safety threshold and the run stops cleanly, not with a crash. That clean stop is itself a real, hard-won result (see below), not the final answer to the control question.
Engineering win
Getting to a clean stop instead of a native process crash took real debugging: the SPH solver can blow up mid-step, inside a control step's ~200 internal substeps—faster than a between-step safety check can catch. Fixed by checking angular velocity after every substep, not just between control steps. This is the first time this project's closed-loop script has ever completed a run without an unrecoverable crash.

Campaign done
The auto-restarting fine-tuning campaign above ran to completion: 524,288 of a 526,336-step target (99.6%), stopped deliberately rather than left to drift. The campaign's own final checkpoint turned out to be regressed, not improved — it survives only 24 steps, far short of earlier checkpoints. Sweeping all 25 saved checkpoints against the real tank found the actual best one is not the most recent: checkpoint 514560 is the only one of the 25 that both survives a full 200-step test and settles to a near-zero final angular velocity (−0.0122 rad/s) — every other surviving checkpoint did so with real residual spin, or right at the safety-trip boundary itself. The trajectory across checkpoints has real structure, not a simple decline: mostly stable, a dip, a recovery, then a sharp late collapse where the policy's own torque output range drops by more than half — a real behavioral change, not just shorter survival. Checkpoint 514560 is now this project's recommended closed-loop policy.

With a best checkpoint identified, the real remaining question was whether its control is actually good, not just non-crashing — answered by running it head-to-head against classical PID and LQR controllers, all three on the identical real closed-loop SPH tank (not the fast surrogate, which uses the wrong torque scale and dynamics for a checkpoint trained this way).

RL wins, with a caveat
The trained policy suppresses sloshing roughly 15× better than PID (0.0010 J vs. 0.0157 J final slosh kinetic energy) — by far the best of the three at the actual task. But it is not indefinitely stable: extending the test window 50% past the sweep's own 200-step length shows even this checkpoint eventually hits the same 1.0 rad/s safety trip, at step 252. PID is the only controller that survives the full window without tripping, though it leaves meaningfully more residual sloshing — a real, honest trade-off, not a clean win for either. This is reported as a known bound on the result: the claim is best-in-class slosh suppression on real fluid within a ~5 s stability window, not an indefinitely stable controller. LQR diverges outright, crashing at step 34 with angular velocity climbing explosively in the run's final five steps. This isn't a bug: LQR's gain matrix comes from linearizing the same Housner-equivalent-pendulum model that Section 02 above already showed correlates weakly with real SPH fluid — this is the first direct demonstration that the mismatch is severe enough to actively destabilize control, not just reduce accuracy. (LQR remains valid for the fast surrogate it was actually designed against.)

Everything above uses the “god-mode” observation—raw fluid position and velocity, information no real sensor could ever provide. A separate campaign fine-tuned the same closed loop against a genuinely hardware-deployable observation instead: only tank IMU readings and a differential wall-pressure proxy, the same sensor set ObservableSloshingEnv already validated on the fast surrogate.

Campaign completed cleanly
16,384 new fine-tuning timesteps (507,904 → 524,288), run across two sessions with zero crashes and zero supervisor restarts the entire way— more stable than the god-mode campaign's own history. That stability made the control-quality question answerable for real, rather than left open by a run that never finished.
A flat sweep, explained by a passive baseline
Sweeping all 64 saved checkpoints against the real tank found something striking: every checkpoint trips the safety limit at nearly the same step (23–27), with no meaningful difference between the earliest checkpoint and the campaign's own final one. Adding a zero-torque passive baseline resolved the ambiguity—it trips at step 22, almost identical to every trained checkpoint. This specific disturbance/torque-limit combination isn't survivable long by any policy, not just this campaign's. The trained policy is measurably, if modestly, better than doing nothing (26 steps vs. 22, and ~19% lower final slosh kinetic energy)—a real signal it learned something—but nowhere close to what the god-mode checkpoint 514560 achieved above.
Ruled out the cheap fixes too
A follow-up, bounded grid—3 torque limits × 3 disturbance magnitudes, using the campaign's own final checkpoint—tested whether an easier setting would change the picture. It didn't: the policy's advantage over passive stayed flat at 4–5 steps across every combination, even doubling torque authority (7 → 14 N·m) and nearly halving the disturbance. Passive survival itself barely moved with disturbance size either—pointing at the tank's own already-documented inverted-pendulum instability (its center of mass sits directly above the pivot, so a small tilt grows on its own under gravity) as the real limiting factor, not a settings choice inherited from the god-mode campaign. Honest conclusion: pressure-only closed-loop control, as fine-tuned here, has not learned to counteract this tank's structural instability—a real, reportable negative result, not a failure requiring more sweeps.
04

Every key number, in one place

How “slosh energy” is measured
For the equivalent-pendulum (Housner convective) model, slosh energy is the mode’s full mechanical energy: kinetic ½·mc·v² plus gravitational potential mc·g·L·(1−cos θ), with mc = 9.70 kg and L = 0.138 m. An earlier version reported the kinetic part only; the potential part is 51–66% of the mode’s energy over the saved runs, so that earlier value under-stated it by about half. Every “~0 J” result still holds with the full energy. For the real SPH fluid, values are the bulk fluid’s kinetic energy (½·M·v² of the fluid’s centre of mass). A potential term is deliberately not added there: the SPH fluid’s centre of mass slowly sinks as a numerical artifact (about 40 mm at dx = 0.010, 0.6 mm at dx = 0.002), and M·g·Δh from that sink would be 3–40× larger than the real sloshing energy at every resolution tested.

05

Answers to the second review

Written answers to the instructor’s second-review points that are not covered by a figure: why the torque is bounded, the problem statement, applications, significance, how the tank was sized, why water, and the three controllers explained for a non-specialist. The free-body diagram, block diagram and PPO flowchart are Figs. 0b–0d in section 00; the hand calculation vs simulation comparison is in the Excel workbook.

1. Why the motor torque is bounded

Short answer: a real motor has a maximum torque, so an unbounded torque would describe a machine that cannot be built and would let the controller "cheat". The limits used were chosen from measurements, and each controller (PID, LQR, PPO) gets the same limit, so the comparison is fair.

1. Every real actuator saturates. A motor's torque is capped by its current rating, its gearbox and its power supply. A controller designed without that cap can ask for torques no motor can deliver. Its simulated results would then not carry over to hardware. Bounding the torque in simulation is the standard way to keep the design physically honest.

2. The fast training model: ±2 N·m, and the policy never comes close to it. In 10 test episodes on the fast surrogate model, the trained PPO policy's largest torque was 0.08–0.19 N·m, under 10% of the 2 N·m limit. Here the bound is a safety rail, not a constraint that shapes the result. (Measured with models/ppo_sloshing, seeds 0–9.)

3. The real-fluid simulation: ±7 N·m, chosen by a measured sweep, not guessed. Two measurements set this limit:

  • The fluid's own push-back. The real SPH water pushes back on the tank with a peak reaction torque of about 4.78 N·m (Entry 42). A limit below that cannot hold the tank against the water, so 7 N·m leaves about 46% margin above it.
  • A torque-limit sweep on the real closed loop (Entry 59), measuring how long the controller keeps the tank under control (out of 300+ steps):
Torque limit (N·m) Survival (control steps) What happens
1.0 ~60 Too weak: tank runs away in one direction
2.0 ~40–50 Marginal, keeps oscillating
4.0 ~100–125 Good control while it lasts
5.0 – 6.0 ~150 Good control while it lasts
7.0 ~200–300 Best region found
8.0 ~200–210 Good, but shorter than 7.0
10.0 ~90–100 Too strong: over-corrects and swings past level

Survival does not keep improving with more torque. Too little torque cannot hold the tank, and too much makes the controller over-correct (classic "too much gain"). 7 N·m is the measured best.

4. Gravity sets a floor too. The tank's centre of mass is 119 mm above the pivot, so gravity pulls it over with a moment of about (m_t·h_t + m_i·h_i)·g·sin θ = 10.7·sin θ N·m. That is ≈1.9 N·m at a 10° tilt. A 2 N·m motor could barely hold that tilt; 7 N·m can.

5. It is a realistic motor size. 7 N·m is in the range of a small industrial servo, or a large (NEMA 34-class) stepper motor. That is what a bench-top rig like this tank would actually use.

Conclusion: the bound is not an arbitrary simplification. It reflects real actuator limits, it is sized from the measured fluid torque, and the value was picked by experiment.

2. Problem statement

When a partly filled container moves, the liquid inside sloshes. That moving mass pushes back on the container with large, oscillating forces, it can spill, and in vehicles it can tip them over.

This project asks: can a learning controller (reinforcement learning) actively tilt a tank so as to cancel its own sloshing, and does that controller still work on realistic, particle-simulated water and not just on the simplified model it was trained on?

The concrete set-up is a 400 × 250 × 300 mm acrylic tank, filled 200 mm deep with water. It is mounted on a single pivot and tilted by one torque-controlled motor. The liquid gets a disturbance, a push or a tilt. The controller sees the tank's angle and angular velocity plus the liquid's state, and every 20 ms chooses a motor torque. Its goal is to bring the sloshing to rest quickly with little motor effort, within the motor's torque limit.

What makes the problem hard:

  • The tank is unstable on its own. Its centre of mass sits 119 mm above the pivot, so it tips over unless something actively holds it (an inverted pendulum).
  • The water and the tank push on each other. Tilting the tank excites the water, and the water's push-back moves the tank.
  • Simple models do not capture real water exactly. A controller tuned on a simple model (like LQR) can fail on the real fluid; this project shows LQR diverging on the realistic SPH water.

3. Where this can be used

Sloshing control matters anywhere a partly filled container is moved or tilted:

Area Why sloshing matters there
Road tankers (fuel, milk, water, chemicals) Sloshing water shifts the load sideways in turns and braking, lowering rollover stability (Zheng et al., 2017).
Ships carrying liquid cargo (LNG, oil) Sloshing loads on tank walls and on the ship's motion.
Aerospace (rocket propellant tanks) Propellant sloshing disturbs vehicle attitude control; the classic reference is NASA SP-106 (Abramson, 1966).
Factory automation (bottling, packaging, liquid-handling robots) Containers must move fast without spilling; slosh suppression lets lines run faster (Reyhanoglu & Rubio Hervas, 2013).
Storage tanks under earthquakes The Housner model used here was created for exactly this case (Housner, 1963).

Application in detail: an actively stabilised liquid tank on a vehicle

Picture a delivery vehicle carrying a partly filled liquid tank, for example a water or milk tanker, or a medical vehicle transporting fluids. Every bump, turn or brake throws the liquid against one wall. That surge can spill the load, damage it, or shift the vehicle's centre of mass at the worst moment.

This project's set-up maps onto that case directly:

  • The tank on a single pivot is the container mounted on a tilting cradle.
  • The motor is the cradle's actuator.
  • The disturbance is the bump or turn, as shown in the 3D lab's "truck bed over a bumpy road" tab.
  • The controller measures the tilt and the liquid's motion and tilts the tank against the surge before it builds up, the way a waiter tilts a tray.

Passive solutions, like baffles inside the tank, add weight and are fixed at design time. An active, learned controller adapts to the actual fill level and motion. The results here show it can suppress real-fluid sloshing far better than a tuned PID controller.

4. Significance: what the results show and where they can be used

  1. Reinforcement learning works on realistic water, not just on the model it learned from. On the particle-resolved SPH simulation, the trained policy left about 15× less sloshing energy than a tuned PID controller (0.0010 J vs 0.0157 J). That held within a stated ~5 s stability window (Entry 80).
  2. A classic model-based controller can fail when the model is simplified. LQR, designed on the equivalent pendulum, diverged within 34 steps on the real fluid. That is direct evidence that learning from interaction helps when the physics is hard to model exactly.
  3. Training on a cheap model, then fine-tuning on realistic physics, is effective. A short fine-tune on real rigid-body physics improved the policy ~3.8×, and longer fine-tuning made it worse. That gives a practical recipe: train cheaply first, then adapt briefly and stop early.
  4. The cheap model is trustworthy within known limits. The Housner pendulum predicts the real fluid's sloshing frequency within ~6% (see the Excel comparison). It does not capture sustained tilts, and the report documents why.
  5. The simulation itself is numerically checked. A 4-resolution convergence study showed the real-fluid results converging (the gap halves at each refinement). So the conclusions are not artefacts of a coarse grid.

Where these results can be used: as a design method for active anti-slosh systems: tilting cradles on tankers, fast liquid-handling robots, and packaging lines. The workflow is: simulate, train, check on high-fidelity fluid, then deploy. The honest limits are part of the result too: the best controller is validated over a ~5 s window, and control from realistic sensors only (wall pressure + IMU) did not yet work. Both are what a hardware follow-up would need to address.

5. How the tank size and values were chosen

Every value lives in config/simulation_config.py (TankConfig, FluidConfig). Each one was picked for a stated reason, listed here.

Quantity Value Why this value
Tank length L (sloshing direction) 0.40 m Bench-top laboratory scale. Model-scale sloshing tests are normally run in tanks of a few tens of cm to about 1 m (Faltinsen & Timokha, 2009; Ibrahim, 2005); for example, Rafiee et al. (2011) validated SPH against a 1.3 m lab tank. 0.40 m sits at the small, desk-top end of that range: cheap to build, fill and film.
Tank width 0.25 m Narrower than the length, so the first sloshing mode is along the length, the one axis the motor tilts. Width only scales the water mass; it does not change the sloshing frequency.
Tank height 0.30 m Leaves 100 mm of freeboard above the water (see below).
Wall thickness 6 mm A standard cast-acrylic sheet thickness.
Wall material Cast acrylic (PMMA), 1180 kg/m³ Transparent, so the free surface can be seen and filmed in a real rig; light; easy to cut and glue. Standard for laboratory sloshing tanks.
Fill depth h 0.20 m Half the length (h/L = 0.5, L/h = 2). See below.
Liquid Water, 1000 kg/m³ See "Why water" below.
Liquid damping 0.5% of critical The standard literature value for the sloshing mode of a smooth-walled water tank (Sivy et al., 2017). The inviscid theory cannot predict damping, so it has to be an empirical input.

Comparable published work (what this set-up is modelled on). Each paper below was checked to exist with these authors and details.

Paper What they did How it relates to this project
Liu, Li, Peng, Zhou & Gao (2024), Water 16, 1551 Lab experiments on a rectangular water tank under pitch (rotational) excitation, at several fill levels and frequencies. Same kind of motion as here: the tank rotates about a pivot instead of sliding. They report violent resonant sloshing at low fill and a "soft-spring" frequency shift at high fill. Both are reasons this project uses a moderate fill.
Akyıldız & Ünal (2005), Ocean Engineering 32, 1503–1516 Measured wall pressures in a pitching rectangular tank, varying fill depth and excitation. Classic experimental reference for pitch-excited rectangular tanks, the configuration used here.
Rafiee, Pistani & Thiagarajan (2011), Computational Mechanics 47, 65–75 Compared SPH simulations with lab sloshing experiments in a rectangular tank. Precedent for using SPH, this project's high-fidelity solver, as a validated sloshing model.
Panigrahy, Saha & Maity (2009), Ocean Engineering 36, 213–222 Lab experiments on sloshing in rectangular tanks with and without baffles. Passive suppression (baffles), the alternative to this project's active control.
Ye, Ren, Zhang, Ma, Hu & Haidn (2025), arXiv:2505.02354 Deep reinforcement learning + SPH to control a movable baffle; mean surface amplitude cut by 81.6%. The closest recent work: RL trained against SPH to suppress sloshing. Here, the RL controller moves the whole tank instead of a baffle.
Feddema et al. (1997), IEEE Control Systems Magazine 17(1), 29–36; Grundelius & Bernhardsson (1999), IEEE CCA; Yano & Terashima (2001), IEEE Trans. Control Systems Technology 9(3), 483–493 Classical control to move open liquid containers without sloshing (robots, packaging machines). The model-based control tradition that this project's PID/LQR baselines represent.

Why fill to half the length (h/L = 0.5)?

  1. The Housner/ACI model is valid there. ACI 350.3-06's curve fits are meant for reasonably proportioned tanks; for very shallow tanks (L/h above about 5) the impulsive-height fit gives meaningless negative heights. L/h = 2 is well inside the valid range.
  2. Both parts of the liquid matter. At this depth the water splits almost evenly into an impulsive part (10.85 kg, moves rigidly with the tank) and a convective, sloshing part (9.70 kg). A controller therefore has a large sloshing mass to deal with, not a token one.
  3. It is a finite-depth tank, not a shallow-water one. Linear theory gives ω² = (gπ/L)·tanh(πh/L); here tanh(πh/L) = 0.92, so the depth still affects the frequency but the flow is not shallow-water (which brings hydraulic jumps and bores that the equivalent-pendulum model cannot represent).

Natural frequency. These choices give a first sloshing frequency of 1.34 Hz (Housner). That is slow enough for a camera and a modest motor to follow and fast enough to settle within a few seconds. The particle (SPH) simulation measured 1.42 Hz, about 6% higher (Entry 95).

Freeboard (100 mm). In the most violent demo run (driven at resonance), the surface tilts about 9–10°. At 10° the water at the wall rises about 0.20 × tan 10° ≈ 35 mm, well under 100 mm, so the water never hits the lid. A lid impact would add a different, strongly non-linear physics that this study does not model.

One honest approximation. For this tank, Housner's impulsive + convective masses add up to 20.55 kg, 2.7% more than the 20.0 kg of water actually in the (outer-dimension) tank. This is a known property of the curve fits, not a bookkeeping error, and the code reports it (modeled_mass_fraction = 1.027).

Why water and not petrol (or another liquid)

Short answer: water is the simplest and safest liquid to start with, and the method carries over to other liquids directly.

  1. Safe on a bench. Petrol is highly flammable and gives off vapour at room temperature. A tank sloshing next to a motor and electronics is a fire risk; water is not.
  2. Well-known, stable properties. Water's density and viscosity are known precisely and barely vary between samples. Petrol is a blend whose properties change with grade and season, which adds uncertainty without adding insight.
  3. It is the standard reference liquid. Housner's model, ACI 350.3 and most experimental sloshing data are for water, so the results can be checked against the literature.
  4. The method does not depend on the liquid. In the equivalent model, the sloshing frequency depends only on the tank shape and fill depth, not on density. Running the project's own Housner code with petrol's density (about 745 kg/m³) gives the same 1.34 Hz; only the masses scale down by about 25% (convective mass 9.70 kg → 7.23 kg). A lighter liquid sloshes at the same rate but pushes less hard, so the motor would need less torque. Petrol's lower viscosity would mean slightly less damping, which a controller has to make up for; that is a change of one input (damping_ratio), not of the method.

Note on viscosity in the realistic-water (SPH) runs (added 2026-10-04). The SPH solver does not use water's real viscosity. With the setting used here (ARTIFICIAL_UNILATERAL), Chrono::FSI damps the fluid only through an artificial-viscosity term (coefficient 0.03 in the one-way runs, 0.1 in the closed-loop runs) and density smoothing; the viscosity value passed to it is ignored. This was confirmed in Chrono's source code. So "realistic water" here means water's real density, free surface and wall interaction, not its real viscous damping, and switching to petrol would change only the density in these simulations.

Future work: repeat the training with a different liquid by changing FluidConfig.density (and the damping ratio) and retraining. No code changes are needed.

6. The three controllers, explained for a non-specialist

What a controller does here. Every 20 ms (50 times a second) the controller looks at the tank and answers one question: how hard should the motor twist the tank right now, and which way? The answer is a torque, capped at the motor's limit (Section 1). The three controllers differ only in how they come up with that answer.

An everyday picture helps: carrying a full bowl of soup across a room. A beginner keeps the bowl level and hopes for the best (PID). An engineer with a formula for how soup moves works out the ideal tilt (LQR). An experienced waiter has carried thousands of bowls and just knows how to tilt against the wave (PPO, the learned controller).

PID: "correct the error you can see"

  • What it looks at: only the tank's tilt angle (and how fast that angle is changing).
  • How it decides: it adds three corrections. P: push back in proportion to how far the tank is from level. I: push a bit harder if the tank has stayed off-level for a while. D: ease off if the tank is already moving back quickly, so it does not overshoot. This project's gains are Kp = 14, Ki = 1.5, Kd = 4.5 (control/pid_controller.py).
  • Strength: simple, needs no model, used in most industrial machines.
  • Weakness: it does not see the water at all. If the water sloshes while the tank stays level, PID sees "no error" and does nothing. On the simplified model, where the push is given to the water only, it applied exactly zero torque for the whole run.
  • Result on the realistic SPH water: the only controller that never lost control in the 6 s test, but it left the most sloshing behind (0.0157 J).

LQR: "solve the optimal answer from a formula"

  • What it looks at: the tank's angle and speed and the water's swing angle and speed (four numbers).
  • How it decides: from the equivalent-pendulum equations of the tank and water, it solves once, in advance, for the best fixed trade-off between "settle quickly" and "use little torque" (a standard method called the Linear Quadratic Regulator). The result is four fixed numbers. Torque = −(6.32 × tank angle + 2.57 × tank speed + 3.84 × water angle − 2.35 × water speed) (control/lqr_controller.py).
  • Strength: mathematically optimal, provided the model is right. On the simplified model it settled the sloshing in about 3.4 s with very smooth torque.
  • Weakness: it is only as good as its model. Real water does not behave exactly like a pendulum.
  • Result on the realistic SPH water: it lost control within 34 steps (0.7 s). This is the clearest evidence in the project that a model-based design can fail on the real physics.

PPO (reinforcement learning): "learn by practice"

  • What it looks at: seven numbers: tank angle and speed, the water's centre-of-mass position and velocity, and the current sloshing energy.
  • How it decides: a small neural network (two layers of 64 neurons) maps those seven numbers to a torque. Nobody wrote its rules. It was trained by trial and error over 500,000 practice steps: after each action it receives a score (penalising sloshing energy, motor effort and tilt), and PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization, a standard training algorithm) adjusts the network a little at a time towards actions that score better. It was then fine-tuned on the realistic water.
  • Strength: it can learn behaviour too complicated to write down as a formula, and it does not need an exact model of the water.
  • Weakness: it is harder to explain why it chose a given action, and it is only tested for the situations it has seen. On the realistic water it stayed in control for about 5 s (252 steps), then lost control; this is reported as a known limit.
  • Result: on the simplified model it settled the sloshing fastest (1.2 s vs LQR's 3.4–3.7 s). On the realistic SPH water it left about 15× less sloshing energy than PID (0.0010 J vs 0.0157 J).

Side by side

PID LQR PPO (learned)
Sees the water? No Yes (through a model) Yes
Needs a model of the water? No Yes No (learns from practice)
How the rule is made Hand-tuned gains Solved from equations Trained by trial and error
Simplified model: settling time Never (does not react) 3.4 s 1.2 s
Realistic SPH water Stays in control, most sloshing left Loses control in 0.7 s Least sloshing (15× less than PID), in control ~5 s

In one sentence: PID is robust but blind to the water, LQR is optimal but trusts a model that real water does not quite follow, and the learned controller suppresses real sloshing best, within a stated time window.

Best closed-loop checkpoint identified & benchmarked; hardware-deployable variant now evaluated too

The fine-tuning campaign referenced above has since run to completion (524,288 of a 526,336-step target) and a full sweep of every saved checkpoint identified 514560 — not the most recent one — as the best usable policy. Benchmarked directly against PID and LQR on the real closed-loop SPH tank: it suppresses sloshing roughly 15× better than PID, though (unlike PID) it isn't indefinitely stable at longer horizons. A genuinely different SPH boundary method (HOLMES) was tested against the wall-penetration issue below and found to meaningfully help containment while costing survival time for an ADAMI-trained policy — and the fair follow-up question (would a policy trained under HOLMES from scratch do better?) has since been answered: a full training campaign hit a reproducible crash trap twice and was closed at 25% progress, and a full checkpoint sweep found that nothing — no HOLMES checkpoint, and not even the best ADAMI checkpoint evaluated under HOLMES — controls the tank well under HOLMES dynamics. ADAMI remains the default and 514560 remains the only validated closed-loop checkpoint. A further campaign trained the same closed loop against a hardware-deployable, pressure-only observation (no raw fluid position) instead of the god-mode one used above — it has since finished and been evaluated (64-checkpoint sweep + a passive-baseline check + a bounded settings grid), and the honest conclusion is a real but modest negative result: it beats doing nothing but has not learned to counteract this tank's own inverted-pendulum instability. See Section 03 above for the full story. Since a hardware-deployable controller is outside the capstone's current scope, this line of work is on hold, not in progress.
